paragraphs: Observational data do not always determine a unique causal effect. When hidden variables leave several causal explanations compatible with the observations, researchers can instead calculate upper and lower bounds. Existing approaches can produce tight bounds, but their polynomial optimization problems become difficult when variables have many possible values.

This paper makes a specific assumption about the hidden variables responsible for that ambiguity: they have small entropy, meaning limited uncertainty in their values. Under this definition of weak confounding, the authors formulate an efficient linear program for bounding the causal effect. The approach incorporates information about the confounders that the comparison methods cannot use.

The authors show that the bounds close together as the confounders’ entropy approaches zero. This gives a precise connection between weakening hidden uncertainty and narrowing causal ambiguity. Simulations using synthetic and real data also produce tighter bounds than existing approaches in settings with weak confounders. The contribution is therefore a computationally practical way to obtain more informative causal ranges under an explicit entropy assumption.
icml-2023-approximate-causal-effect-iden.tldr: An efficient linear program bounds otherwise unidentified causal effects more tightly when the relevant hidden confounders have small entropy.

paragraphs: Auditing a language model requires finding concrete situations in which it behaves unexpectedly. This paper treats that search as an optimization problem: specify a behavior of interest, then search for an input and corresponding output that satisfy it. A target might combine an innocuous input with an offensive completion, making both sides of the interaction relevant.

Such searches are difficult because text consists of discrete choices, successful examples may be sparse, and the models themselves are large and nonlinear. The proposed algorithm, ARCA, addresses these challenges by optimizing inputs and outputs jointly. This makes the desired response part of the search procedure alongside the prompt that could elicit it.

The authors demonstrate searches that uncover derogatory celebrity completions, French inputs followed by English outputs, and prompts that elicit a particular name. These findings illustrate different kinds of behavior that a targeted audit can expose. ARCA offers a promising method for discovering failure cases before deployment; the reported contribution is an automated search tool for those cases.
icml-2023-automatically-auditing-large-l.tldr: ARCA jointly searches over prompts and completions to automatically uncover targeted unexpected behaviors in language models.

paragraphs: Molecular optimization aims to generate molecules with desirable properties, but evaluating the generator presents its own statistical problem. A common workflow learns a property predictor from a sample of molecules, uses that predictor to guide generation, and then uses it again to assess the generated molecules. The paper asks how reliable that resulting performance estimate is.

The theoretical analysis identifies two potential sources of bias. One arises when the predictor is misspecified, so its model of the target property is inadequate. The other arises from reusing the same finite sample for training and evaluation. These are distinct problems: an evaluation can be affected by the predictor’s assumptions, by the reuse of observations, or by both.

The authors discuss ways to reduce each source of bias and investigate their effectiveness empirically. Their contribution concerns the credibility of the evaluation process as well as molecular generation itself. In particular, a favorable score from the predictor used during optimization needs to be interpreted with attention to how that predictor and its evaluation data were constructed.
icml-2023-biases-in-evaluation-of-molecu.tldr: The paper identifies two potential biases in predictor-based molecular optimization evaluation and investigates ways to reduce them.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can extract useful representations from large unlabeled datasets, but processing every example becomes increasingly expensive. This paper investigates which examples matter most for contrastive learning, with the aim of selecting smaller training sets that preserve the usefulness of the learned representation.

The authors prove that the most valuable examples for this setting are those whose augmented versions are most similar to other examples, in expectation. They also give guarantees for generalization when contrastive learning uses subsets selected on this basis. The result connects an example’s value to relationships between augmented data, providing a principled criterion for deciding what to retain.

Experiments remove 20% of CIFAR100 and 40% of STL10 and TinyImageNet without reducing downstream task performance. The selected subsets generally outperform random subsets by over 3% across these datasets. The authors also find that examples most useful for contrastive learning contribute least to supervised learning. This means that the training objective matters when judging data value: a subset valuable for one learning setup may have very different value for another.
icml-2023-data-efficient-contrastive-sel.tldr: Selecting examples by expected similarity between augmentations reduces contrastive learning data needs while preserving downstream performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: An out-of-distribution detector tries to recognize inputs outside the classes represented in a pretrained model’s training data. Some inference-time methods assume that such inputs should receive equal probabilities across all known classes. The paper shows that this assumption causes those methods to fail when the model was trained on unequal numbers of examples per class.

By analyzing causal relationships between classes and features, the authors identify several common scenarios in which unfamiliar inputs should instead follow the known classes’ prior distribution. That distribution reflects their relative prevalence. They propose replacing an explicitly used uniform distribution with this class prior, or reweighting detection scores using similarity between the prior and the model’s softmax output.

Experiments show that both modifications can improve detection when the pretrained model learned from imbalanced data. The finding gives class prevalence a concrete role in interpreting a model’s response to unfamiliar inputs. Its scope is qualified: the causal analysis identifies scenarios supporting the prior-based distribution, rather than asserting that every out-of-distribution input must follow it.
icml-2023-detecting-out-of-distribution-.tldr: Accounting for training-class prevalence can improve inference-time detection of unfamiliar inputs when the pretrained model learned from imbalanced data.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning adapts a pretrained masked language model using a task prompt and a verbalizer that connects predicted tokens to output labels. With few labeled examples, the prompt’s starting point matters. The paper argues that a single shared initialization cannot adequately serve every task and example when tasks are complex.

MetaPrompter replaces that single starting point with a pool of prompts learned through meta-learning. Attention constructs prompts that depend on the individual input, allowing the pool to supply different combinations of task knowledge. The method also introduces RepVerb, a soft verbalizer that builds label embeddings directly from feature embeddings, changing how the model’s representations connect to classification labels.

Only the prompt pool requires tuning, making the approach parameter-efficient compared with the cited method that tunes the entire masked language model. Experiments report better performance than recent competing approaches, while RepVerb separately outperforms existing soft verbalizers. Together, the findings support using adaptable prompt structure and feature-based label representations to make better use of limited labeled data.
icml-2023-effective-structured-prompting.tldr: MetaPrompter combines input-dependent prompts from a learned pool with feature-based label embeddings to improve parameter-efficient few-shot prompting.

paragraphs: Neural networks that respect symmetries often achieve this by restricting their internal architecture. Depending on the task, an output should either remain unchanged under a transformation or change in a corresponding way. This paper proposes learning a canonical representation of the input as another route to obtaining those symmetry properties.

A learned canonicalization function can be attached to a backbone that is not itself equivariant. The authors give explicit constructions for several transformation groups and show that the approach has universal approximation capabilities. This arrangement makes the learned choice of canonical representation an interpretable component of the system, while allowing flexibility in the backbone architecture.

The central hypothesis is that a small network can learn canonicalization more effectively than predefined heuristics; experiments support that claim. Across image classification, N-body dynamics prediction, point cloud classification, and part segmentation, the method is competitive with existing equivariant approaches and faster throughout the reported comparisons. These results support learned canonicalization as a practical way to introduce symmetry handling across several kinds of tasks.
icml-2023-equivariance-with-learned-cano.tldr: Learned canonicalization adds symmetry handling to ordinary neural backbones and achieves competitive performance with faster execution in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects becomes difficult when the descriptive information about study participants has a complex structure, such as images. The paper introduces Causal Multi-task Deep Ensemble, or CMDE, to address this setting. Its design learns information shared across the study population alongside information specific to individual groups, preserving both kinds of structure in the estimation process.

The authors establish a theoretical connection to multi-task Gaussian processes: before observing data, CMDE is equivalent to a process with a coregionalization kernel. This links the ensemble to a model that represents relationships between tasks. Compared with the multi-task Gaussian process approach, CMDE efficiently handles high-dimensional covariates and combinations of different data modalities.

CMDE also provides pointwise uncertainty estimates, giving uncertainty information alongside causal-effect estimates for individual points. Across datasets and tasks, it outperforms state-of-the-art methods on a majority of the evaluated tasks. The result supports the framework’s usefulness for structurally complex data while retaining the reported qualification that its empirical advantage does not cover every task.
icml-2023-estimating-causal-effects-usin.tldr: CMDE combines shared and group-specific learning to estimate causal effects and pointwise uncertainty from complex, high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Understanding several treatments used together requires estimating their joint effect. Directly studying many treatment combinations can demand large samples, and some combinations may involve unsafe interactions. This paper develops methods for using information spread across multiple experimental datasets to estimate these combined effects.

The first contribution concerns identification: determining whether the available experimental distributions contain enough information to compute the joint treatment effect. The authors derive new conditions for making that determination under several scenarios. This separates the question of whether an effect can be recovered from the question of how to estimate it using a finite collection of observations.

The second contribution is a set of estimators with properties including consistency and robustness to model misspecification and slow convergence. Simulation studies support the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The practical significance is a framework for combining experiments when its identification conditions apply, with statistical methods designed to tolerate specified estimation difficulties. The conditions remain central because combining datasets alone does not establish that a particular joint effect is recoverable.
icml-2023-estimating-joint-treatment-eff.tldr: The paper gives identification conditions and robust estimators for recovering joint treatment effects from multiple experimental datasets.

paragraphs: Fair representation learning preprocesses data so that classifiers trained on the resulting representations can behave more fairly. A practical certificate goes further than an observed fairness score: it gives a provable upper bound on the unfairness of any downstream classifier using those representations. FARE is designed to provide such certificates.

The key choice is to restrict the encoder’s representation space. That restriction makes useful guarantees possible while still allowing favorable accuracy–fairness tradeoffs for suitable implementations. The authors propose an implementation based on fair trees and develop a statistical procedure that turns finite data into a high-confidence upper bound on downstream unfairness.

In the experimental evaluation, FARE’s certificates are tight and often comparable to the purely empirical results reported by earlier methods. This matters because a bound that is much looser than observed behavior can offer little practical guidance. The reported results show that restricting representations can yield assurances that remain informative, while the certificate’s finite-sample, high-confidence character specifies the statistical form of that assurance.
icml-2023-fare-provably-fair-representat.tldr: FARE restricts learned representations to produce practical, high-confidence bounds on the unfairness of any downstream classifier.

paragraphs: A classifier can learn a misleading shortcut when a biased visual cue strongly accompanies the target label. Correcting that behavior is especially difficult when examples without the bias are rare or unavailable. CDvG addresses this situation without explicitly requiring bias labels or bias-free examples.

The method starts from the observation that image translation models, like classifiers, tend to focus on these harmful biases. It uses an image translation model to change one form of bias into another while preserving information relevant to the task. Contrastive learning then uses the transformed views to learn representations that remain consistent across changes in the bias.

The authors report stronger debiasing as the bias becomes more severe, and their method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse datasets, particularly when bias-free examples are extremely scarce or absent. CDvG can also be combined with methods that emphasize available bias-free samples for further improvement. Its central contribution is to turn a generative model’s sensitivity to bias into a source of training variation that supports learning less bias-dependent representations.
icml-2023-fighting-fire-with-fire-contra.tldr: CDvG changes biased image cues through generation and uses contrastive learning to reduce shortcut reliance without explicit bias labels or bias-free samples.

paragraphs: Unnormalized statistical models assign scores whose conversion into probabilities requires a partition function, which can be expensive to handle. Noise-contrastive estimation avoids this difficulty by learning to distinguish real observations from artificial noise. However, its objective can be flat and slow to optimize, motivating the paper’s direct approach to negative log-likelihood.

The authors introduce a noise distribution that lets them express the log partition function as a composition of functions. The inner function can be estimated from stochastic samples, making stochastic compositional optimization applicable. This preserves a likelihood-based objective while providing a computational route through the troublesome normalization term.

The analysis establishes a fast convergence rate and relates the influence of the noise distribution to the variance of the stochastic estimates. For one-dimensional Gaussian mean estimation, the authors show a more favorable objective landscape and faster convergence than noise-contrastive estimation. Experiments also report improvements in density estimation, out-of-distribution detection, and real image generation. Together, these results connect the optimization formulation to both theoretical behavior and performance in several applications.
icml-2023-learning-unnormalized-statisti.tldr: Rewriting normalization as a stochastic compositional problem enables direct likelihood training with theoretical and empirical advantages over noise-contrastive estimation.

paragraphs: People can learn a word’s meaning after only a few exposures, even without explicit feedback. MEWL turns this ability into an evaluation problem for machines: given limited examples of words in visual scenes, how effectively can a model work out what those words refer to? The benchmark targets grounded word learning as a component of multimodal understanding.

The suite contains nine tasks designed around abilities emphasized in developmental accounts of children’s learning. These include reasoning across situations, using other available structure to support learning, and pragmatic learning. Organizing the evaluation around these capabilities allows the authors to probe several aspects of word acquisition within a common few-shot setting.

The paper evaluates agents that use multiple modalities as well as agents that use a single modality, and compares their performance with humans. The authors observe a sharp divergence between human and machine word learning. MEWL’s contribution is therefore both a structured benchmark and evidence that progress in multimodal systems leaves substantial differences in how people and machines acquire word meanings from limited exposure.
icml-2023-mewl-few-shot-multimodal-word-.tldr: MEWL uses nine few-shot tasks to evaluate word learning in visual scenes and reveals sharp differences between human and machine performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing three-dimensional shapes requires representing both surface geometry and topology, including changes in connectivity. Explicit template methods are constrained by a fixed topology, while implicit methods can handle varied topology but need expensive point sampling. NeuralSlice represents a 3D surface as the intersection of a four-dimensional tetrahedral mesh and a slicing hyperplane.

The network learns both how to deform the 4D template and how to set the slice. A spatially aware component uses positional encoding to relate 4D points to a 3D feature volume, allowing local geometric information to guide deformation. Moving the representation into four dimensions lets a single template support different resulting shapes and topologies.

The method guarantees manifold meshes and surpasses state-of-the-art explicit approaches in reconstruction quality. Compared with the implicit approaches evaluated, it is ten times faster and better preserves thin structures, with its efficiency attributed to avoiding point sampling. These findings show how a higher-dimensional construction can provide flexible surface topology while retaining an efficient route to an explicit triangle mesh.
icml-2023-neuralslice-neural-3d-triangle.tldr: NeuralSlice reconstructs flexible-topology 3D meshes by slicing a learned 4D mesh, improving quality and speed in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Mean-field theory provides simplified predictions about neural networks, but relating those predictions to networks of finite width requires controlling approximation error. This paper studies that relationship at initialization for deep multilayer perceptrons with batch normalization. Its focus is on Gram matrices, which summarize relationships between hidden representations.

A central concern is that small discrepancies introduced at individual layers might grow as depth increases. The authors show that batch normalization avoids this amplification. They then establish a concentration bound describing agreement with a mean-field model when the sequence of hidden representations is rapidly mixing. That mixing condition is an explicit requirement of the bound.

The authors describe their result as the first such concentration bound for standard finite-width multilayer perceptrons that remains informative as depth grows. The significance is that the theoretical approximation need not become useless simply because the network is deep. The analysis concerns random networks at initialization, with the rapid-mixing condition specifying when the stated concentration guarantee applies.
icml-2023-on-bridging-the-gap-between-me.tldr: Batch normalization prevents depth-driven error amplification in the studied mean-field approximation, with a finite-width concentration guarantee under rapid mixing.

paragraphs: Geometric graphs describe objects whose nodes occupy positions in Euclidean space, including molecules and materials. Assessing a network’s ability to distinguish such graphs requires accounting for permutations, rotations, reflections, and translations. This paper develops a geometric version of the Weisfeiler–Leman test, called GWL, to study expressive power while respecting these symmetries.

The framework clarifies consequences of architectural choices. Invariant layers cannot distinguish geometric graphs that look identical within one-hop neighborhoods. Equivariant layers can distinguish a larger class by carrying geometric information beyond those local neighborhoods. The analysis also shows how higher-order tensors and scalarization enable maximally powerful geometric graph networks.

The authors connect this ability to distinguish graphs with universal approximation, establishing an equivalence between the two perspectives in their framework. Synthetic experiments supplement the theoretical results. The contribution is a systematic explanation of why symmetry-respecting architectures differ in capability: preserving and propagating geometric information affects which structures a network can tell apart, and that discrimination power is tied to the functions it can represent.
icml-2023-on-the-expressive-power-of-geo.tldr: A geometric Weisfeiler–Leman framework explains how symmetry handling and geometric information propagation determine geometric graph networks’ expressive power.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions among options whose hidden states evolve independently according to Markov chains. Rewards depend on both the selected option and its current state. The decision maker knows neither the transition rules nor the reward functions, and choosing an option does not reveal its state. Learning must therefore rely on observed actions and rewards.

TSEETC combines Thompson sampling with episodes that grow longer over time. Each episode begins with exploration, selecting options in round-robin order and updating a posterior represented as a mixture of Dirichlet distributions. For exploitation, the algorithm samples model parameters from that posterior and follows the sampled model’s optimal policy for the remainder of the episode.

The authors prove a Bayesian regret bound that grows approximately as the square root of the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors. Simulations also show lower regret than existing algorithms. The result supports a structured alternation between gathering information and committing to a sampled policy, even when the system’s evolving states remain unobserved throughout learning.
icml-2023-online-restless-bandits-with-u.tldr: TSEETC learns from actions and rewards alone in hidden-state restless bandits, achieving a Bayesian regret bound of approximately square-root growth.

paragraphs: Code-generating language models can produce errors that developers must repair or subtle bugs they may overlook. R-U-SURE addresses how to communicate uncertainty in suggestions when the developer’s intended result is unknown. It treats samples from a generative model as proxies for different possible user intents and evaluates suggestions according to their usefulness across those possibilities.

The method combines minimum-Bayes-risk decoding, dual decomposition, and decision diagrams to construct structured uncertainty summaries efficiently. Its requirements are sample access to a code generator and, optionally, a parser for abstract syntax trees. This makes the uncertainty mechanism usable with an arbitrary generative code model without requiring retraining.

The authors demonstrate the approach on three developer-assistance tasks and apply it to different interaction patterns. It produces more accurate uncertainty estimates than the token-probability baselines evaluated. The contribution is to make uncertainty depend on the utility of a structured suggestion under plausible user goals, connecting what the assistant presents to the range of outcomes the user may actually want.
icml-2023-r-u-sure-uncertainty-aware-cod.tldr: R-U-SURE builds structured uncertainty summaries for code suggestions by evaluating their utility across sampled proxies for possible user intents.

paragraphs: Compositional reinforcement learning builds long tasks from sequences of smaller subtasks, each handled by its own policy. The challenge studied here is to train those policies so they remain useful across different task sequences. The authors focus on maximizing performance on the worst sequence, making robustness across compositions the training objective.

They formulate learning as a two-agent zero-sum game. One side learns the subtask policies, while an adversary selects the sequence of subtasks. This makes difficult compositions part of the optimization process. The paper proposes two algorithms: an adaptation of existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods and an asynchronous version that allows subtask policies to train in parallel.

Evaluation in two multi-task environments with continuous states and actions shows improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. These experiments support the proposed training strategy for producing more robust reusable components. The objective targets worst-case performance across tasks, while the reported empirical finding is improved performance in the two tested environments; it does not establish successful execution of every possible sequence.
icml-2023-robust-subtask-learning-for-co.tldr: Adversarially choosing subtask sequences trains reusable reinforcement-learning policies toward stronger worst-case compositional performance.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns how well a model’s confidence reflects the reliability of its predictions. This paper links unreliable confidence to differences in training loss across classes. Those differences can arise because visual variation within and between classes makes some classes easier to fit than others, leaving uneven patterns of overfitting and underfitting.

The proposed method uses separate scaling factors for each class to reduce variation among their training losses. It balances the losses of overfitted classes against those of underfitted classes while preserving the integrated training loss. The framework can be incorporated into post-hoc calibration methods, starting from a pretrained model to reduce the additional computation needed.

Across several post-hoc methods, the approach generally improves calibration while preserving classification accuracy. The authors also report good performance with unbalanced datasets and untuned hyperparameters. The stated findings support treating differences between class-level fitting behavior as a useful calibration signal, with the loss-balancing construction intended to improve confidence reliability while maintaining the model’s predictive performance.
icml-2023-scaling-of-class-wise-training.tldr: Balancing class-specific training losses generally improves post-hoc confidence calibration while preserving accuracy in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Organizing a product catalog involves both grouping products and arranging the groups. The input set can vary in size, the number of groups is not fixed, and constraints on group sizes can also vary. The paper calls this combination the Catalog Problem and uses it to study adaptive ordered clustering.

Neural Ordered Clusters, or NOC, is a modular, fully differentiable architecture that joins clustering with learning an order. It includes a mechanism for learning constraints on the number of items in each cluster. Combining these decisions in one model addresses the interaction between group membership, group size, and the arrangement of the resulting groups.

The authors evaluate NOC on three datasets, including synthetic catalog structures and PROCAT, a real catalog dataset containing more than 1.5 million products. They report state-of-the-art results on a new, more challenging formulation of the problem and also examine higher-order interactions. The contribution is a unified learning approach for outputs that must vary in both their grouping structure and their ordering.
icml-2023-the-catalog-problem-clustering.tldr: NOC jointly learns how to cluster variable-sized sets, satisfy cluster-size constraints, and order the resulting groups.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling chooses among uncertain options using samples from posterior reward distributions. This paper proposes epsilon-Exploring Thompson Sampling, which uses that decision rule only with a user-selected probability epsilon. Otherwise, it chooses greedily according to observed mean rewards. Epsilon is a fixed value strictly between zero and one.

Reducing posterior-based exploration improves computational efficiency while retaining the original posterior update structure. The authors prove both minimax and asymptotic optimality for several common reward distributions, including Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson, and Gamma. These guarantees describe strong regret behavior in both worst-case and long-run senses for the covered settings.

A key analytical change relaxes a demanding anti-concentration requirement on the posterior that appeared in recent analyses. This enables the guarantees with fewer algorithmic alterations, avoiding machinery such as clipping sampling distributions or inverting a divergence between reward distributions used in previous work. Empirical evaluations support the method’s efficiency and optimality. The result shows that this particular reduction in exploration can preserve strong theoretical performance while making the algorithm faster and simple to implement.
icml-2023-thompson-sampling-with-less-ex.tldr: Mixing greedy decisions with occasional Thompson sampling improves speed while achieving minimax and asymptotic optimality for several common reward distributions.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to make a network withstand deliberately chosen input changes within a specified size limit. This paper focuses on changes bounded by the l1 norm. The authors show that training for this setting is more prone to catastrophic overfitting and instability than training against l2- or l-infinity-bounded changes.

Their analysis connects these difficulties to coordinate descent, the strategy used by existing methods to construct updates. They introduce Fast-EG-l1, an efficient adversarial training algorithm based on Euclidean geometry that avoids coordinate descent. The method adds neither memory costs nor extra hyperparameters to tune, making the stability intervention compatible with an efficiency-focused training setup.

Experiments across several datasets find that Fast-EG-l1 delivers the strongest and most stable l1 robustness among the compared methods with similar computational complexity. That comparison scope matters: the reported advantage concerns methods operating at comparable computational cost. The contribution combines an explanation for a specific source of training instability with an algorithm that improves the observed robustness–efficiency balance.
icml-2023-towards-stable-and-efficient-a.tldr: Fast-EG-l1 avoids coordinate descent to improve the stability and robustness of efficient adversarial training against l1-bounded attacks.

paragraphs: Gradient descent is thought to favor solutions that generalize well even without an explicit instruction to do so. This paper examines its learning dynamics in matrix sensing, where the objective is to recover a low-rank matrix from near-isotropic linear measurements. The setting provides a concrete way to study how solution complexity develops during optimization.

With a small initialization, gradient descent follows an incremental pattern resembling greedy low-rank learning. It learns solutions of increasing rank sequentially as it moves toward recovering the ground-truth matrix. The analysis characterizes the full progression of learning, extending earlier work that described only the initial phase associated with rank-one solutions.

The authors also analyze incremental behavior in the under-parameterized regime, expanding beyond the over-parameterized setting emphasized in much prior work. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings. The significance is a detailed account of how gradient descent can build increasingly complex structure over time in this matrix-sensing setting, with small initialization and the stated measurement structure central to the result.
icml-2023-understanding-incremental-lear.tldr: For matrix sensing with small initialization, gradient descent learns progressively higher-rank structure through an incremental process characterized beyond its first phase.

paragraphs: Robot tasks can be specified through language, a visual goal, or a demonstration, and these formats are often handled by separate models. VIMA brings a wide range of manipulation tasks into a common format: prompts that interleave text and visual tokens. This lets different forms of task instruction enter the same robot agent.

The authors build a simulation benchmark with thousands of procedurally generated tabletop tasks, more than 600,000 expert trajectories, and four levels of generalization evaluation. VIMA uses a transformer to process multimodal prompts and generate motor actions autoregressively. The benchmark and agent together provide a way to study both learning efficiency and transfer to unfamiliar tasks.

In the hardest zero-shot generalization setting, VIMA achieves up to 2.9 times the task success rate of alternative designs using the same training data. With ten times less training data, it still performs 2.7 times better than the best competing variant. These reported comparisons support the proposed design’s data efficiency and generalization within the simulation benchmark.
icml-2023-vima-robot-manipulation-with-m.tldr: VIMA uses interleaved text and visual prompts to guide one robot agent across manipulation tasks, with strong generalization and data efficiency in simulation.
